text: Your team designed three versions of a landing page and randomly assigned visitors to each. Are the three average order values genuinely different? With two groups you'd use a t-test. With three or more, you use ANOVA, analysis of variance. Despite the name, it tests means, by comparing kinds of variability.

Why not just run several t-tests? Three groups need three pairwise tests, five groups need ten, and every extra test is another chance for a false alarm. ANOVA asks one question first: is there any difference among these means? It compares between-group variability, how far group means sit from the overall mean, to within-group variability, the noise inside each group. That ratio is the F statistic. Near one means noise; large means real differences.

In Python, f underscore oneway takes the groups. Sixty simulated visitors per design, averaging fifty, fifty-four and sixty. F is seven point three five nine, and p is point zero zero zero nine. We reject the null that all three means are equal.

Here's the same result from first principles. Sum of squares between groups: seventeen sixty-four. Within groups: about twenty-one thousand. Divide each by its degrees of freedom, take the ratio, and you get seven point three six. Eta squared is the share of variability explained by group: about seven point seven percent. The design matters, but most variation is still individual differences.

A significant ANOVA doesn't say which groups differ. Tukey's HSD compares every pair while controlling the overall false-alarm rate. Here A versus C is clearly different, p about point zero zero zero six. A versus B is point two eight, B versus C is point zero six. Not significant doesn't mean the same.

Assumptions. Observations should be independent. Each group should be roughly normal, or large enough for the central limit theorem to help. Group variances should be similar. If those look shaky, the rank-based Kruskal-Wallis test is a common alternative; here it agrees, with p of point zero zero one six.
Next up: the deeper problem behind why we didn't just run many t-tests, multiple comparisons.
